text-scene.text: Life on SQL Island had become almost predictable. SQLaus knew the roads between the villages, the villagers knew his face, and the island’s tables had become familiar enough to feel trustworthy.

That routine changed one morning when several sealed crates and wrapped bundles of documents were discovered at the shore near Onionville. No ship had been seen during the night, and no villager claimed to know where the delivery had come from. Yet the contents were unmistakably deliberate: copied ledgers, valuation lists, and carefully structured catalogue fragments connected to a collector of rare objects.

“These are not ordinary island records,” SQLaus said after reading the first few pages. A short note accompanied the archive material: “A true collection is not merely counted. It is ordered.” The signature identified the sender simply as the Collector.

The message was short but the material itself revealed a very clear intention. Certain inhabitants had been marked as unusually interesting, some villages appeared repeatedly in the records, while others were mentioned only in passing. As SQLaus read further, he realized that the archive was not designed to produce simple totals, but to preserve order, rarity, and relative position. Some entries had to be ranked within categories, others compared to earlier or later acquisitions, and several only became meaningful when viewed in the context of the records around them. A summarized result would have hidden exactly the structure that made the archive valuable.
He folded the note and looked back at the catalogue pages. “To analyze this archive, I will need window functions.”

select-scene.text:
Mission 1: Cataloguing the Inhabitants -> Endrit
The Collector first wants a stable archive order. SQLaus must assign a sequential catalogue number to every inhabitant within each village, ordered alphabetically by name.
Tables: Inhabitant, Village Functions: ROW_NUMBER() with PARTITION BY, ORDER BY
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT v.name AS village_name, i.name AS inhabitant_name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER ( PARTITION BY i.villageid ORDER BY i.name ) AS catalogue_number FROM Inhabitant i INNER JOIN Village v ON i.villageid = v.villageid;

select-scene.text:
Mission 2: Ranking the Most Valuable Curiosities -> Endrit
The Collector wants a global prestige ranking of all inhabitants by gold. If two inhabitants have the same amount, they should share the same place, with gaps in the following rank positions.
Tables: Inhabitant, Village Functions: RANK() with ORDER BY
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT i.name AS inhabitant_name, v.name AS village_name, i.gold, RANK() OVER ( ORDER BY i.gold DESC ) AS prestige_rank FROM Inhabitant i INNER JOIN Village v ON i.villageid = v.villageid;

select-scene.text:
Mission 3: Compact Village Display -> Rino
For a cleaner public exhibition, the Collector wants inhabitants ranked by gold within each village, but without skipped positions after ties.
Tables: Inhabitant, Village Functions: DENSE_RANK() with PARTITION BY, ORDER BY

Mission 4: Comparing Consecutive Acquisitions -> Rino
The archive reveals a sequence of acquisitions. SQLaus must compare each acquisition’s estimated value with the previous acquisition in the same category to show how the archive evolved.
Tables: CollectorArchive (new), Inhabitant, Village Functions: LAG() with PARTITION BY, ORDER BY
new table: CollectorArchive(entryid, category, villageid, personid, estimated_value, rarity_score, recorded_day)

manipulate-scene.text:
Mission 5: Updating the records with the next Acquisition.
The Collector wants to see which entry comes next in each category, according to the record date. Because there is an empty column in the records for a key pointing to the next item, SQLaus wants to add said information into the concerning column namednext_entryid. This should make the archive more comprehensible.
manipulate-scene.sql-solution: WITH next_entries AS ( SELECT entryid, LEAD(entryid) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY recorded_day) AS next_entryid FROM CollectorArchive ) UPDATE CollectorArchive ca SET next_entryid = ne.next_entryid FROM next_entries ne WHERE ca.entryid = ne.entryid;
manipulate-scene.sql-check:
WITH next_entries AS ( SELECT entryid, LEAD(entryid) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY recorded_day) AS next_entryid FROM CollectorArchive )
SELECT ca.entryid, ca.next_entryid FROM CollectorArchive ca INNER JOIN next_entries ne on ca.entryid = ne.entryid where ca.next_entryid = ne.next_entryid;

select-scene.text:
Mission 6: First Relic and Latest Relic -> Joël
After browsing through the archive documents for a while, SQLaus wonders, how the different Categories developed over time. In order to do so, he wants to see the first, and last entry per category, one row per category to keep things tidy.
Giving it some thought, SQLaus decides that the following columns should be displayed: - category - first_description - first_recorded_day - first_estimated_value - last_description - last_recorded_day - last_estimated_value
select-scene.sql-solution:
WITH cat_first_last AS ( SELECT DISTINCT category,
FIRST_VALUE(entryid) OVER ( PARTITION BY category ORDER BY recorded_day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS first_entryid,
LAST_VALUE(entryid) OVER ( PARTITION BY category ORDER BY recorded_day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS last_entryid
FROM CollectorArchive ) SELECT cfl.category, ca_first.description AS first_description, ca_first.recorded_day AS first_recorded_day, ca_first.estimated_value AS first_estimated_value, ca_last.description AS last_description, ca_last.recorded_day AS last_recorded_day, ca_last.estimated_value AS last_estimated_value FROM cat_first_last AS cfl INNER JOIN CollectorArchive AS ca_first on cfl.first_entryid = ca_first.entryid INNER JOIN CollectorArchive AS ca_last on cfl.last_entryid = ca_last.entryid ;

select-scene.text:
Mission 7: The Third-Rarest Standard -> Lana
While studying the Archive, SQLaus noticed that the Collector does not compare items randomly. Instead, he uses a fixed benchmark: the third entry in descending rarity within each category.
“This is the standard,” SQLaus murmurs. “Not the rarest… but the point of balance.” To understand the Collector’s logic, SQLaus must display every archive entry together with this benchmark value for its category.
Display the following columns: - category - description - rarity_score - third_highest_rarity
Tables: CollectorArchive Functions: NTH_VALUE() with PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT category, description, rarity_score, NTH_VALUE(rarity_score, 3) OVER ( PARTITION BY category ORDER BY rarity_score DESC, entryid ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS third_highest_rarity FROM CollectorArchive;

select-scene.text:
Mission 8: The Collector's Prestige Tiers -> Lana
To present the archive more clearly, the Collector wants each category divided into three prestige tiers based on estimated value. SQLaus must assign every archive entry to its tier within the category, with the most valuable entries placed in tier 1.
Display the following columns: - category - description - estimated_value - prestige_tier
Tables: CollectorArchive Functions: NTILE() with PARTITION BY, ORDER BY
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT category, description, estimated_value, NTILE(3) OVER ( PARTITION BY category ORDER BY estimated_value DESC, entryid ) AS prestige_tier FROM CollectorArchive;
